derives_from: 외래어 표기법 (문교부 고시 제85-11호, 1986-01-07; maintained by the National Institute of Korean Language), 제2장 표 1 국제 음성 기호와 한글 대조표 -- the IPA-to-Hangul correspondence table the regulation names as the basis of all its other tables and as the default for any language not separately tabulated, read off its two columns (모음 앞 | 자음 앞 또는 어말). 제1장 제1항 (the 24 modern jamo only) and 제2항 (one phoneme, one symbol) are kept as written, and 제9항 supplies the 반모음 rows. 제5항 (established forms win) is honoured by `data/respell/overrides`, which outranks this file.

deviations.rule: 제3항 -- a 받침 may only be ㄱ ㄴ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ
deviations.why: Kept, and now a decision rather than a limitation, since NFC makes a 받침 expressible. **Written as a 받침:** ㄴ for /n ɳ ɴ/, ㅁ for /m/, ㅇ for /ŋ/ and for the nasality of a nasal vowel, ㄹ for /l ɫ ɭ ʎ/ -- always, so 뱅크, 힌트, 램프, 호텔, 콘, 생크, 융, 앙팡. And ㅂ ㅅ ㄱ for a /p t k/ after a short vowel, which is 영어 세칙 제1항's condition in full -- 짧은 모음과 유음·비음 이외의 자음 사이, so word-finally *and* before another obstruent: 캣, 북, 크랍, 디껏, 액트, 픽처, 엑스. ㅅ also serves a geminate stop, which is 일본어 세칙's 촉음 rule: 칩푸, 캇테. **Written as its own ㅡ syllable** -- the 대조표's 자음 앞 또는 어말 column -- everything else: the fricatives (스 즈 프 브 흐), the affricates (츠 지 치), the voiced stops (브 드 그), any /p t k/ that fails the short-vowel test (에스트, 데스크, 마스크, 카르트), and the rhotics, because the 대조표 gives [l] a ㄹ 받침 but [r] the syllable 르 (포르 파보르, 베를린). Only the first consonant of a coda can take a 받침, Hangul having one 종성 slot, which is exactly why 힌트 and 뱅크 come out right. Of the seven, ㄷ ㅈ ㅊ ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅎ never appear, and ㅅ stands for a final /t/ because the 받침 neutralises to [t].

deviations.rule: 제3항, the one place a 받침 is refused on phonological grounds
deviations.why: A word-final stop keeps the ㅡ form when a 유음 or 비음 follows it in the same coda, which is 영어 세칙 제1항's own exclusion (짧은 모음과 유음·비음 이외의 자음 사이). Korean phonology says why: 받침 ㅅ ㄱ ㅂ assimilate before ㄹ ㅁ ㄴ, so votre as 봇르 would be read [본느]. 보트르 it is. A slot cannot look ahead within itself, so each stop-plus-liquid pair is one rule.

deviations.rule: 제4항 -- 파열음 are never written with 된소리
deviations.why: Relaxed, but only in an onset and only where the target's own inventory proves an aspiration contrast (`if_inventory: "pʰ"` and its siblings), which today means Mandarin, Thai and Hindi. The Institute's own newsletter grants that an unaspirated voiceless stop is nearer 된소리 than the aspirated series 제4항 mandates, and gives as its reason that one transcriber would have to adjudicate the aspirated/tense boundary across Greek, Turkish, Dutch, Arabic, Thai and Hindi -- a cost an inventory predicate does not pay. Korean lax stops are voiceless unaspirated word-initially and voiced between vowels, so the pair that writes an unaspirated voiceless stop in *both* positions is lax initially and tense elsewhere: 라-꼰 for /laːkɔːn/, 마이-뻰-라이 for /majpenraj/. The standard sets its own precedent for position-conditioned letters in the 일본어 세칙, where か行 is ㄱ word-initially and ㅋ mid-word. In a coda the block is a bare ㅡ syllable where the tense letter buys nothing and reads oddly, so the 대조표 is kept there: /baːt/ is 바트, not 바뜨. 제4항 covers 파열음 only, so the ㅉ of /tɕ/ and /ts/ is inside the standard, and is what its own 중국어 표기 세칙 prints (마오쩌둥).

deviations.rule: 제4항, continued -- targets whose inventory cannot prove the contrast
deviations.why: Not relaxed, and this is a considered disagreement with `content/RESPELL-SYSTEMS.md`, which names Spanish, French, Italian, Japanese, Thai and Vietnamese as reading better with ㅃㄸㄲ. Thai is covered above; the other five have no aspirated series in phonemic IPA, and neither does English or German, whose /p t k/ *are* aspirated and must stay ㅍㅌㅋ. The data holds no discriminator, so the choice is between printing the standard's answer and hard-coding four language codes in a `targets` block. We print the standard's: /toːkjoː/ is 토-쿄 where a Korean reader expects 도쿄. If the owner wants the survey's list it is six rules per target in `targets` (p t k -> lax when word_initial, tense otherwise). Vietnamese needs no rule at all -- its `ipa` column is simply missing the /tʰ/ of th-, and the moment it has it these rules fire on their own.

deviations.rule: 제9항 다만 -- after a consonant, [w] is written as its own syllable (트위스트), except after [ɡ], [h] and [k] (쿼터, 펭귄)
deviations.why: Applied as written for a non-tonal target, and reversed for a tonal one (`unless_inventory: "˧"`). The clause is written for European consonant clusters; the same IPA string in Mandarin, Vietnamese and Thai is a medial glide inside one syllable, and splitting it would invent a syllable in a language whose syllable count is morphemic -- 说 /ʂwɔ/ must be 숴, not 스워. Lexical tone in the `ipa` column is the one thing in the data that tracks the difference, the medial being a property of exactly those syllable canons. So /twɪst/ is 트위스트, /bwaʁ/ 브와르, /kwatɾo/ 콰트로.

deviations.rule: 제9항 -- [ʃ] and [ɲ] are 시 and 니 before a vowel, merged into the ㅑ series
deviations.why: Merged for the four plain groups where the merge is worth its rules -- ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ, so 샤 셔 쇼 슈 냐 녀 뇨 뉴, which is what makes 뉴료쿠 and 아뇨스 -- and left unmerged elsewhere, because the merge needs the 초성 rule to know the whole nucleus and each group costs a rule per consonant plus a suppression rule per vowel. Before an /i/-like vowel nothing is needed (시, 니 fall out of the bare 초성), but /ʃɛ/ is 세 rather than 셰 and /ʃɑ̃/ 상 rather than 샹.

deviations.rule: the language-specific 세칙 of 제3장 (영어, 일본어, 중국어, 프랑스어 …)
deviations.why: Not applied as tables; only 표 1, the IPA table 제2장 names as the basis of the others and as the default for anything not tabulated. The 세칙 are indexed by the source language's own spelling, which is the index this feature cannot have, and they contradict each other on the same IPA -- 일본어 세칙 writes か as 가/카 by position, 중국어 세칙 writes pinyin b as ㅂ and z as ㅉ. Two of their conditions are borrowed above, because both are phonetic rather than orthographic and so survive the change of index: 영어 세칙 제1항's 짧은 모음 test for a final stop, and 일본어 세칙's ㅅ 받침 for a geminate. Where a 세칙 form is the one a Korean reader expects, it belongs in `data/respell/overrides`, which 제5항 makes authoritative over this file anyway.

deviations.rule: the 대조표 has no row for tone, length or palatalisation
deviations.why: Chao tone letters are dropped (`tone: "drop"`): the standard marks no tone, and a Korean reader cannot read them. Length is dropped -- the survey's length table gives Hangul "none", the Seoul contrast is dead for younger speakers, and the 대조표 has no long-vowel row. Russian palatalisation (`ʲ`) is dropped rather than written 니/랴, which costs 덴 nothing but flattens сь and зь.

note:
Hangul is a composing script, and since `word()` in `core/respell.js` normalises each assembled syllable to NFC, the three slots really are 초성/중성/종성: this table emits conjoining jamo and the engine composes them into one precomposed block. `syllable_fixups` is empty -- with NFC there is nothing left for it to do.

Two invariants hold the table together, and both are about what a 받침 may attach to. **A vowel is always conjoining jamo** -- the 중성 alone when a 초성 is waiting for it (`after_out` lists the 19 초성), ᄋ plus the 중성 when it opens a block of its own, which covers an onsetless syllable and the second element of a diphthong alike. Never the precomposed character, because a 받침 can only reach a 중성 that is still loose: this is what makes /jʊŋ/ 융 and /el/ 엘. **A consonant's own ㅡ block is precomposed**, for the mirror reason -- a 받침 must not reach back into it, or /dɛsk/ would be 데슥 instead of 데스크.

A 초성 is otherwise written bare so the vowel can bind to it, but a bare 초성 with nothing after it would ship as an isolated jamo glyph and leave its own syllable out of the font subset -- a box in the PDF. Two positions therefore give it a whole block instead: inside an onset cluster, where the previous 초성 is still open and Korean's own ㅡ epenthesis is the right answer (/str/ is 스트르 + ᅵ = 스트리, the prescribed form), and a word with no vowel at all, such as Russian в or Arabic mkbːr, spelled `if_nucleus: " "` because that is the only way to ask the engine whether the nucleus is empty.

`max_onset` is 1, which is what Korean phonotactics want -- a Korean syllable admits exactly one 초성 and no cluster at all -- and it is measurably the best value now that the syllabifier segments on phonemes rather than codepoints: against 2 or 3 it spends 309 fewer syllables on the same 11,807 rows and writes 320 more 받침, because a consonant it leaves in the coda can become a 받침 where the same consonant pulled into the next onset has to carry its own ㅡ block. Arabic's article is the clearest case: 알-바크-시시, not 아-르바크-시시.
